1.pericope_label: Joseph bought into Potiphar's house and set over it

schools.summary: Gill grants that the master knew nothing of the spiritual and gracious presence of God and was no judge of it, but perceived by the ingenuity of Joseph's mind, his ready and speedy learning of the Egyptian language, and his dexterity and faithfulness in everything, that here was an extraordinary person for his age. Calvin puts the theology under the verse: it is never well with men except so far as the Lord shows himself gracious to them, for though he vouchsafes his blessing for a time even to reprobates he meanwhile curses their felicity, so that what they took for the height of fortune turns to ruin; the world forms for itself a goddess of fortune, or else each man adores his own industry, but Scripture teaches that adversity is a sign of God's absence and prosperity of his presence. He adds a caution against reading the verse too grandly, since Joseph was not at once elevated but is reckoned among the slaves and holds his life subject to his master's will, so that we should learn even amid our sufferings to perceive the grace of God, content to have our cup mingled with some portion of sweetness. Of Potiphar's perception Calvin makes more, since the grace of God shone out so plainly that it became manifest even to a heathen, blind in this respect — from which he concludes that heathens may be so affected by religion as to be constrained to ascribe glory to God; yet the man's ingratitude betrays itself at once, for he despises the God whose gifts he estimates so highly in Joseph, and ought at least to have inquired who that God was instead of deeming it enough, so far as it was to his private advantage, to acknowledge that his slave was divinely directed. From Joseph's beauty Calvin draws the sober moral that we should not greatly desire those graces of person which conciliate the favour of the world, seeing how readily Satan turns the gifts of God into snares to catch souls.

Henry calls the purchase a good bargain, whatever Potiphar gave for him, better than the merchandise of silver, and quotes the Jewish proverb that if the world did but know the worth of good men they would hedge them about with pearls. He turns the servitude into consolation: Joseph's brethren had stripped him of his coat of many colours but could not strip him of his virtue and prudence, and those who can separate us from all our friends cannot deprive us of the gracious presence of our God. Wesley repeats both sentences almost word for word, and adds that the master knew not aught he had save the bread which he did eat, the servant having all the care and trouble of the estate and the master only the enjoyment of it — an example not to be imitated by any master, unless he could be sure of having a Joseph for his servant.

Clarke explains the office Joseph was given, the Hebrew verb meaning to visit, take care of, superintend, and answering to the Greek word from which we have overseer or bishop. He also reports how far Joseph's beauty travelled, being celebrated over all the East, with Mohammed devoting a whole chapter of the Koran to him and the Persian poets Jamy and Nizamy each writing a poem on Joseph and Zuleekha, as the Asiatics call Potiphar's wife.
Keil states the turn of the chapter baldly: Joseph was handsome in form and feature, and Potiphar's wife set her eyes upon the handsome young man and tried to persuade him.

debates.question: What did Potiphar actually perceive when he saw that the Lord was with Joseph?

positions.position: nothing spiritual, of which he was no judge, but the ingenuity of Joseph's mind, his quick learning of the language, and his dexterity in business
the grace of God shining out so plainly that even a heathen was constrained to ascribe glory to God — though he never asked who that God was

outliers.note: follows Joseph's beauty out of scripture and into the literature of the East, where the Koran gives him a chapter and the Persian poets a pair of romances

themes: the Lord with him in the house of the Egyptian
what Potiphar could and could not see
a beauty that became a danger

schools.summary: Gill prefers to read Joseph's boast the other way — not that he was greater than his fellow servants, but that his master himself was not greater in the house than he, having a larger propriety in it but no larger use of it. Calvin supposes the account compressed, since Moses touches only the chief points and there is no doubt that this impure woman tried various arts upon the pious youth, insinuating herself by indirect blandishments long before she broke out into so shameless a licence. He finds the finer point in the form of Joseph's argument, that he acknowledges himself the more strictly bound the greater the power entrusted to him — ingenuous men having this property, that the more is confided to them the less they can bear to deceive — and adds that he would not seem restrained only by regard to man, and so declares that the act would offend God, since nothing is more powerful to overcome temptation than the fear of God. Of the daily repetition Calvin says the constancy shows a real fear of God reigning in him, since he not only repelled one attack but stood forth to the last the conqueror of all; and he notes how easily we fall when Satan tempts us through another, seeming exempt from blame if the one who induces us bears a part of it.

Henry traces the whole affair to a look, since her sin began in the eye, and warns that remarkable beauty often proves a dangerous snare both to its owner and to others, so that we have great need to make a covenant with our eyes lest the eye infect the heart — she had a husband who ought to have been to her a covering of the eyes from all others. What followed he calls daring and shameless, for where the unclean spirit gets dominion in a soul the clothes of modesty are thrown off and the bands of shame broken in pieces, and lust once headstrong will stick at nothing and blush at nothing. He rates Joseph's escape, all things considered, as great an instance of the divine power as the deliverance of the three children out of the fiery furnace, and lists what was ranged against him: the tempter was his mistress, whom it was his place to obey and his interest to oblige, and whose enmity he courted at his peril; and Satan, finding he could not overcome this man with troubles and the frowns of the world, assaulted him instead with soft and charming pleasures, which have slain their ten thousands.

Clarke numbers the two reasons Joseph gives — gratitude to the master to whom he owed all that he had, and fear of the God in whose sight it would be a heinous offence — and asks how, with the kindness of the one and the displeasure of the other before his eyes, he could have committed an act that would at once have marked him the most ungrateful and the most worthless of men. Wesley presses the last clause hardest: not only how shall I sin against my master, my mistress, myself, my own body and soul, but against God? Gracious souls, he says, look upon this as the worst thing in sin, that it is against God, against his nature and his dominion; and they that love God for this reason hate sin. From the words that Joseph would not so much as be with her, Wesley draws the practical rule that those who would be kept from harm must keep themselves out of harm's way.
Keil marks the phrase that turns the story, literally about this day — the day the writer has in mind.

debates.question: Which reason weighs most in Joseph's refusal?

positions.position: two stand together — gratitude to a master who had given him everything, and fear of the God in whose sight it would be heinous
the fear of God is decisive, since nothing is more powerful to overcome temptation, and Joseph names it lest he seem restrained only by regard to man
that it is against God is the worst thing in sin, and gracious souls hate sin for that reason above all

outliers.note: measures the escape against the fiery furnace, arguing that Satan, having failed to overcome Joseph with troubles and the frowns of the world, assaulted him with pleasures, which have slain their ten thousands

themes: a sin that began in the eye
the two reasons for the refusal
a temptation renewed day by day

11.pericope_label: The garment seized, and the charge reversed

schools.summary: Gill gathers the guesses about the day — a week, a month, or rather a year after she first began, as Aben Ezra reckoned; a public festival which the women attended, on Josephus's account, from which she excused herself by pretending illness; a noted day at the idol's temple, on Jarchi's — noting that on any of them she knew Joseph would be at home and not there, and judged it a fit opportunity. He supposes she seized his garment because he had learned to get away as soon as she began to speak, so that only by holding him could she gain a hearing. Calvin calls this the crisis of the combat, since Joseph had already shown a memorable constancy, a youth tempted through a long succession of days who at an age to which intemperance is commonly pardoned was more moderate than almost any old man, and now the woman openly raves, so that the more arduous the contest the more worthy of praise is a magnanimity that remains inflexible. He states exactly what Joseph stood to lose: he saw that he must incur the danger of losing both his character and his life, chose to sacrifice his character, and was prepared to relinquish life itself rather than be guilty of such wickedness before God — from which Calvin turns on the excuses men make of their reputation, since no one proves that he heartily loves virtue but he who, content with God as his only witness, does not hesitate to submit to any disgrace rather than decline from the path of duty. He also sees a design in her calling the servants at all, since she who had before sought secrecy now summons her domestics, so that by this prejudging of the case she may condemn the youth before ever her husband hears it, and by involving her husband in the charge compel him, for shame, to avenge her.

Henry marks the turn as a change in the passion itself: now her love was turned into the utmost rage and malice, and she pretends she cannot endure the sight of him whom a while ago she could not endure out of her sight, for chaste and holy love will continue though it is slighted, whereas sinful love, like Amnon's to Tamar, is easily changed into sinful hatred. He notices that she calls her husband neither her husband nor her lord but only he, having forgotten the covenant of her God that was between them, and draws the hard conclusion that innocence itself cannot secure a reputation, since not every one who keeps a good conscience can keep a good name. Wesley says that Joseph would not stay to parley with the temptation but flew from it with the utmost abhorrence, leaving the garment behind him as one escaping for his life.

Clarke reads her opening words as a calculated stroke at a husband she did not greatly love — he hath brought in a Hebrew unto us, that is, he raised this person to all his dignity and eminence and so gave him the greater opportunity to mock us — and notes that the word rendered mock is the one used of Isaac and Rebekah, a familiarity allowable only between man and wife.

Keil puts the reversal plainly: when the daring assault upon his chastity had failed on account of his faithfulness and fear of God, the adulterous woman reversed the whole affair and charged him with an attack upon her modesty, to have her revenge and avert suspicion from herself; and in doing it she does not think her husband worth naming, while a Hebrew man was no ornamental epithet to Egyptian ears.

debates.question: Why did she call the servants before telling her husband?

positions.position: to prejudge the case and condemn Joseph before her husband heard it, and to involve her husband so that shame would compel him to avenge her
to have her revenge and avert suspicion from herself, reversing the charge she had earned onto the man who refused her

outliers.note: hears the phrase he hath brought in a Hebrew unto us as aimed at the husband as much as at Joseph, and identifies the verb rendered mock as one used elsewhere of a familiarity proper only between man and wife

themes: a character sacrificed to keep a conscience
the accusation as a mirror of the crime

16.pericope_label: The tale told to Potiphar, and his wrath

schools.summary: Gill follows the small deliberate steps by which the charge was built: she laid up the garment beside her as a proof of what she laid to his charge and as a testimony against him, keeping it until her lord came home, and when he came she told him the affair in much the same manner and to the same import as she had told it to the men of the house, so that the two accounts should answer one another. The cry she reports he glosses as she would have it understood, that she lifted up her voice for help from the servants, frightened at an insolent attempt; and he does not let the sentence stand without naming it for what it was, since the story she related to her husband was her own invention, and a lie. Calvin divides the blame for its being believed. Seeing that so probable a colour had been given to the transaction, it is no wonder that jealousy, whose motions are exceedingly vehement and ardent, prevailed so far with Potiphar as to make him credit his wife's calumnies; what cannot be excused is the levity with which he instantly thrust into prison a servant he had found prudent and honest, without examining the cause. He ought to have been less under the influence of his wife, and received the just reward of his too easy folly by cherishing with honour a harlot in the place of a wife — from which Calvin warns husbands in particular that they must use prudence lest they be carried rashly hither and thither at the will of their wives. He also disposes of an objection raised against the story, that Potiphar is called an eunuch and could have felt no jealousy: in the East the word was used not only of those who were so in fact but of satraps and nobles, so that it means here no more than that he was one of the chief men of the court. Of the sentence itself Calvin says Moses expressly condemns the rashness of a man who took fire as soon as he had heard his wife and gave the reins to his indignation just as if the guilt had been proved, since by that course all equity is excluded, no just defence is allowed, and the true and accurate investigation of the cause is utterly rejected.

Henry looks at the same silence from Joseph's side and finds two possible reasons, either that he durst not make his defence by telling the truth, since it would have reflected too heavily upon his mistress, or that his master would not hear him or would not believe him; and there was no remedy, for he is condemned to perpetual imprisonment. Yet Henry sees a restraint even in the anger, since God held back that wrath, or it would have put Joseph to death, and the wrath which imprisoned him God afterwards made to turn to his praise. He adds that many an action of false imprisonment will in the great day be found to lie against the enemies and persecutors of God's people, and that our Lord Jesus, like Joseph here, was bound and numbered with the transgressors.

positions.position: the procedure allowed none; Potiphar took fire as soon as he heard his wife and gave the reins to his indignation as if the guilt were proved
either Joseph durst not tell the truth, since it would have reflected too heavily on his mistress, or his master would not hear or believe him

outliers.note: answers the objection that a man called an eunuch could feel no jealousy, since in the East the word covered satraps and nobles and here means only that Potiphar was one of the chief men of the court

themes: a sentence passed without a hearing

20.pericope_label: Joseph in the round house, and the keeper's trust

schools.summary: Gill wonders that the sentence was no worse, since as captain of the guard Potiphar had power to imprison of himself and as chief of the executioners it is much that he did not in his passion hand Joseph over to be put to death at once; perhaps something of his old respect survived the impeachment, or he had heard Joseph's apology before committing him, though for his wife's credit he took this step, or else things were so overruled by the providence of God. Of the place itself he notes that the Hebrew word carries the sense of roundness and may be rendered the round house or round tower. He measures the keeper's trust by what the man stopped doing, since he did not inquire into or examine the management, nor take any account of what was in Joseph's hands, the Targums paraphrasing the clause to mean that he saw no crime in him. Calvin agrees that the beginning was severe, since Moses does not say how Joseph was afflicted at first but we readily gather that he was allowed no liberty and thrust into some obscure dungeon, the keeper being under Potiphar's power and at his disposal — and what clemency could be hoped from a man jealous and carried away with the vehemence of his anger? He insists on the sequence that follows: the Lord purposely suffered Joseph to be reduced to extremity, that he might bring him back as from the grave, for as the light of the sun is most clearly seen when we look out from a dark place, so in the darkness of our miseries the grace of God shines more brightly; and that the keeper became humane at all he ascribes to a mind not spontaneously disposed to equity being divinely inclined to it, since God governs the hearts of men according to his will. Calvin then raises the question the narrative leaves open, why the keeper did not fear Potiphar's displeasure and why Potiphar, who could easily have interfered, allowed a man he mortally hated to be treated so kindly: his cruelty may have been divinely restrained, but it is also probable that he had come to suspect his wife's subtle scheme, and that though appeased towards Joseph he was unwilling to acquit him to his own dishonour. What Calvin admires most comes last, that when Joseph is made guard of the prison and has the free administration of it, he nevertheless makes no attempt to escape but waits for the proper season of his liberation.

Clarke agrees that the prison was probably built in the round form its name suggests, and closes the chapter with two reflections of his own: that it is of little consequence where the lot of a servant of God may be cast, since like Joseph he is ever employed for his master and God prospers his work; and that a woman of that spirit is capable of any evil, for when she could not get her wicked ends answered she began to accuse — which is precisely Satan's custom, who first tempts men to sin and then charges them with having committed it, even where the temptation has been faithfully and perseveringly resisted. Wesley, following Henry, thinks Potiphar chose this prison because it was the worst, for there the irons entered into the soul, but God designed it to pave the way to Joseph's enlargement; and he adds that God despises not his prisoners, and can raise up friends for them where they little expect any.

Keil describes the arrangement precisely: the keeper was the governor of the prison, himself under Potiphar as captain of the guard, and it was Jehovah who procured Joseph favour in his eyes, so that he entrusted all the prisoners to his care.

debates.question: Why was Joseph treated so well in a prison under Potiphar's own authority?

positions.position: God inclined a mind not spontaneously disposed to equity, and Potiphar had probably come to suspect his wife's scheme though he would not acquit Joseph to his own dishonour
God can raise up friends for his people where they little expect any, since he despises not his prisoners
Jehovah was with Joseph and procured him favour in the governor's eyes, so that all the prisoners were entrusted to him

outliers.note: reads Potiphar's wife as a figure of Satan's method, who first tempts men to sin and then accuses them of it even where the temptation was faithfully resisted

themes: the round house and why it was chosen
a keeper divinely inclined to kindness
a jailer who would not escape
